questions.prompt: You connect an MCP server and the loop now calls it like any built-in tool. Where does the description of what that server can do actually come from?
options: The server answers tools/list with names, descriptions, and argument schemas, and Claude Code puts those in the window
The host hardcodes a copy of the server's tools at install time, so the server never needs to answer
The model infers the tools by calling the server and reading the errors
The server writes its tools into CLAUDE.md when you approve it
questions.explanation: Discovery is a protocol round-trip: the client asks the server what it has, and the descriptions become tool definitions in the context window — which is why the model picks from a typed menu instead of improvising a command line. Option B describes a plugin, where the host really does ship a static manifest; MCP deliberately moved that out of the host. Option C would work only as a last resort and produces exactly the guesswork MCP exists to remove. Option D is not a thing — CLAUDE.md is prose the agent reads, not a tool registry.

questions.prompt: You need the agent to be able to look up a customer record on demand during a task. Which MCP surface fits, and why?
options: A resource, because content you attach yourself is safer than an action the model can take by itself
A tool, because anything the agent might reach for mid-task has to be callable without you typing it
A prompt, because prompts are the only surface that can read from a database
A tool is required — resources can only reference local files, never remote records
questions.explanation: The deciding question is who triggers it. The model triggers tools, so anything it may need mid-task is a tool. Option A inverts the rule: resources are the safe surface precisely because only you can invoke them with @server:protocol://path. Option C is wrong on the facts — prompts are canned task shapes, they read nothing on their own. Option D is the interesting wrong one because it is half true: resources can reference remote content, but that doesn't make them the right surface for an on-demand lookup.

questions.prompt: A teammate commits a .mcp.json to the repo. You clone it and start Claude Code in that folder. What happens, and what is the actual risk being managed?
options: The servers connect silently — .mcp.json is just config, like any settings file
Claude Code prompts before using project-scoped servers, and a cloned repo cannot approve its own, so the code does not run until a human says yes
The servers load only after a network round-trip to the vendor confirms their signatures
The servers are blocked entirely and can never be used from a cloned repo
questions.explanation: A project-scoped .mcp.json can carry a stdio command that runs arbitrary code with your permissions, so approval is a human gate and settings committed to the repo are ignored in an untrusted folder. Option A is the intuition MCP exists to break: config and executable are not the same category. Option C describes something Claude Code does not do today — there is no signature check on MCP servers. Option D is too strong; reset-project-choices and an interactive approval both bring them back.

questions.prompt: Why is a server described as having its own client, instead of Claude Code talking to servers directly?
options: Because JSON-RPC requires a separate socket per peer, so the client object is just the protocol library
Because each client owns exactly one connection, one handshake, and one failure — which is what lets one server die without taking the others down
Because the model can only make one tool call at a time, so servers take turns
Because clients can be swapped at runtime without restarting the host
questions.explanation: The one-client-per-server boundary is the isolation seam: a broken handshake, a timeout, or a crash in one server is contained to that connection, and the host can show it as one failed entry instead of a dead session. Option A is technically true and practically irrelevant — the socket isn't the reason the object exists. Option C is wrong; the loop interleaves servers freely. Option D is not true of the standard CLI path.
